title: Sleep in Peace: An Evening Prayer of Trust
summary: David asks God to answer him, then turns to rebuke people who drag his honor through the mud and chase after lies. He urges them to be still, to offer right sacrifices, and to trust the LORD. The psalm ends with a joy deeper than a good harvest and the quiet confidence of a man who can lie down and sleep because God keeps him safe.
story: Psalm 4 stands right after Psalm 3, and the two are best read as a pair. Psalm 3 is a morning prayer (“I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me”), and Psalm 4 is an evening one that closes with the same bed and the same sleep. Together they set the tone for the first book of the Psalter (Psalms 1 to 41), where David, the anointed king of Psalm 2, speaks again and again from trouble. The king whom God has promised to establish is not spared opposition. He learns, in public and in private, to hand his reputation and his safety to God. Psalm 4 moves that story forward by turning the prayer outward: David doesn't only ask for help, he speaks to his opponents and invites them to trust the same God.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David, who reigned over Israel from about 1010 to 970 BC. Unlike Psalm 3, it gives no occasion. Some interpreters have connected it with the same period as Psalm 3, the rebellion of David's son Absalom (2 Samuel 15 to 18), when David's honor was publicly attacked and many in Israel turned away. Others read the “How long” of verse 2 against a drought or failed harvest, since verse 7 compares God's gift of joy with abundant grain and new wine, and the complaint of verse 6 (“Who can show us the good?”) sounds like people disappointed with their God.

The headings themselves are an old question. They are part of the Hebrew text as it has come down to us, and the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament made in the last centuries BC) already has them. Many scholars think they were added by the editors who collected the Psalter rather than by the original poets, and that the short Hebrew phrase usually rendered “of David” can mean by David, for David, about David, or belonging to a Davidic collection. Others take the traditional view that the headings preserve reliable memory of authorship. Either way, the editors wanted this prayer read in David's voice.
cultural:
The heading, “For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments”, shows that the psalm was used in Israel's worship, most likely at the temple in Jerusalem, with a leader of music and a string accompaniment. The word Selah, which appears twice here, is a technical term whose meaning is lost. It may mark a musical pause, a raising of the voice, or a place where the congregation responded. Readers today often pause briefly at it, which is a reasonable guess.

Verse 5 assumes Israel's system of sacrifice: animals, grain, and drink offerings brought to God's altar as worship, thanksgiving, and atonement. “Sacrifices of the righteous” means offerings made with a right heart and in keeping with God's law, not ritual performed to manipulate him. Verse 7 speaks from an agricultural world, where the grain harvest and the new wine of the grape harvest were the high points of the year, times of feasting and relief. Verse 6 echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26, in which the LORD makes his face shine on his people. To have God's face shine on you meant his favor, his attention, and his peace.
literary: The psalm is an individual prayer of trust, with elements of lament. It opens with a direct address to God (verse 1), turns to speak to human opponents (verses 2 to 5), reports what “many” are saying and answers them with a prayer (verse 6), and ends with two sentences of personal confidence (verses 7 and 8). The Selah markers after verses 2 and 4 divide the middle section. Hebrew poetry works mainly by parallelism, where a second line restates, sharpens, or extends the first: “love vanity” is paired with “seek after lies”, and “lie down” with “sleep”. The movement from day's noise to night's stillness is part of the design. The bed appears twice, first as the place to search one's heart (verse 4) and then as the place of peaceful sleep (verse 8).

outline.t: Heading and opening plea: answer me, God of my righteousness
To the slanderers: the LORD has set apart his own
Be still, sacrifice rightly, and trust

doctrines.note: The psalm shows prayer as honest speech to a God who has already acted (“You have relieved my distress”) and is asked to act again. It also shows that prayer can include speaking truthfully to others about God, and that it ends in rest rather than anxiety.
Trust here is practical: it is the ability to lie down and sleep while the situation is unresolved. Verse 5 joins trust to worship, and verse 8 names God alone as the source of safety.

The opponents “love vanity and seek after lies”, a phrase that can describe false gods as well as false accusations. The psalm contrasts that empty pursuit with the real good that comes from God's face.

words.note: Tsedeq, righteousness. “God of my righteousness” (verse 1) can mean the God who is himself righteous or the God who will vindicate David's cause. In the Psalms righteousness is less an abstract moral quality than right relationship and right order, and God's righteousness often means his faithful action to set things right for those who are wronged.

Chasid, godly or faithful one. The word is related to chesed, God's covenant love, and describes a person who belongs to God and answers his loyalty with loyalty. In verse 3 the LORD has “set apart the godly for Himself”: the point is not that they are impressive but that God has claimed them.

Shalom, peace. The word covers much more than the absence of conflict: wholeness, safety, well-being, and right relationship. In verse 8 it describes the sleep of someone whose enemies are still there but who is held by God.

christ: Paul quotes the opening words of verse 4 in Ephesians 4:26, “Be angry, yet do not sin”, following the Greek translation, as guidance for life in the church. More broadly, the psalm is the prayer of God's anointed king under slander, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the king who was falsely accused and yet entrusted himself to the Father. The connection is a pattern rather than a prediction: David's trust anticipates the trust of the Son. The Gospels also record Jesus asleep in a boat during a storm while his disciples panicked (Mark 4:38), a scene that echoes the peace of verse 8, and he offers his followers a peace the world does not give.

hard.q: Is anger wrong if the psalm says “Be angry, yet do not sin”?
hard.a: The Hebrew verb in verse 4 means to tremble or be stirred, and translators divide over whether it means “tremble” (with fear or awe) or “be angry”. The Greek translation took it as anger, and Paul used that reading in Ephesians 4:26. On that reading the verse doesn't forbid anger; it assumes anger will come and forbids letting it turn into sin. The rest of the verse supplies the discipline: go to bed, search your heart, and be still. On the other reading, David is telling his opponents to tremble before God and stop sinning. Both readings end in the same place, a quieting of the heart before God.

questions: David is slandered and still sleeps in peace. What would have to be true for you to rest while your reputation or future is unresolved?
Verse 7 says God gives a joy greater than a good harvest. What good things in your life compete for the place of that deeper joy?
The psalm speaks to its opponents, not only about them. How might you speak truthfully and graciously to someone who has wronged you?
